title: LLM Evaluation
oneLiner: Measuring LLMs is tricky because there are many good answers; we combine word-overlap scores, meaning-based scores, benchmarks, fact checks, AI judges and human reviewers, each with blind spots.

what.html:
How do you know if a model, prompt or RAG system is good? Options: perplexity (how surprised the model is by real text), overlap scores like BLEU and ROUGE (shared words with a reference), meaning scores like METEOR and BERTScore, benchmarks and arenas, fact checks for hallucinations, LLM judges, and human evaluation. Each answers a different question.

Everyday versionJudging essays: you could count words matching a model answer (fast but crude), ask a teaching assistant to grade with a rubric (scalable but biased), check every fact (thorough), or have expert teachers read them (best but slow and costly).

why.html:
• Every improvement needs to be measured.
  • The wrong metric gives confident but wrong conclusions.
  • Leaked test questions can make models look better than they are.

how.title: Why it's hard
how.html: Many valid answers, many qualities to judge, and test sets that drift into training data. No single number is enough.

how.title: Perplexity
how.html: If the model's average surprise is 2.3 (in log units), perplexity is e^2.3 ≈ 10: like choosing among 10 equally likely words. Lower is better.

how.title: Count shared words
how.html: Candidate "the cat sat on a mat" shares 5 words with the 8-word reference: precision 5/6 = 0.83, recall 5/8 = 0.625, F1 = 0.71.

how.title: Credit similar meanings
how.html: METEOR counts synonyms ("feline" for "cat"); BERTScore compares meanings via embeddings, so good paraphrases aren't punished.

how.title: Benchmarks and arenas
how.html: Standard question sets compare models cheaply; arenas let people vote between two answers and rank models like chess players (Elo).

how.title: Check every fact
how.html: Split an answer into small claims and verify each: 3 of 4 supported gives 0.75. For RAG, check claims against the retrieved text.

how.title: AI judges
how.html: A strong model grades answers quickly, but tends to favour the first answer shown or the longer one. Swap the order and use clear rubrics.

how.title: People, and leaked tests
how.html: Human raters are the gold standard but slow. And if test questions appeared in training data, scores are inflated, so check for overlap.

demo.html: Pick the right evaluation method for each need.

example.html:
Elo ratings. Two models start at 1500. A wins: each was expected to win half the time, so A gains 16 (1516) and B loses 16 (1484). If A wins again, it gains a bit less (1531), because that win was now expected.

Supplementary Small score differences between models are often within noise; good reports include confidence intervals and multiple runs.

misunderstandings: Lower perplexity means a more helpful chatbot.
High BLEU means a correct answer.
They have position and length biases.
A top benchmark score proves capability.
Leakage and format effects can inflate it.
takeaways: BLEU precision + brevity; ROUGE recall (P 0.83, R 0.625, F1 0.71).
LLM judges need bias controls; humans and leakage checks complete the picture.
thirty: Evaluating generation is hard: many valid outputs, many quality dimensions, saturation and leakage. Perplexity = exp(average NLL) (2.3 → 10), for language-model comparison on the same tokenizer only. BLEU: clipped n-gram precision × brevity penalty; ROUGE: n-gram recall and LCS (5 shared words: P 5/6 = 0.83, R 5/8 = 0.625, F1 0.71); they reward wording, not meaning. METEOR adds stems/synonyms and recall weighting; BERTScore uses embedding similarity (paraphrases score well). Benchmarks: static (cheap, saturate, leak), live, human arenas with Elo (1500/1500 → 1516/1484 after a win), and model-graded. Faithfulness: atomic-fact verification (3/4 = 0.75), RAG faithfulness, relevance and context metrics. LLM-as-a-judge scales but has position, verbosity and self-preference biases: swap orders, rubrics, calibration. Human evaluation is the gold standard (guidelines, multiple raters, agreement). Leakage: detect n-gram overlap, use private and dynamic sets.

check.q: Average NLL 2.3 corresponds to a perplexity of about…
Recall of 5 matched words against an 8-word reference?

opts: Test items appeared in training data
